clinicalPearls: Mucolipidosis II is a severe autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by biallelic GNPTAB mutations that abolish the activity of GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase (its alpha and beta subunits).

Loss of this enzyme prevents attachment of the mannose-6-phosphate recognition marker to newly made lysosomal hydrolases, so the enzymes are mis-secreted into the circulation instead of being delivered to lysosomes.
The hallmark biochemical signature is markedly raised activity of multiple lysosomal enzymes in serum together with correspondingly deficient activity inside cultured fibroblasts.
Cultured fibroblasts contain dense phase-bright cytoplasmic inclusions, the 'inclusion cells' or I-cells that give the disorder its name.

The clinical picture resembles Hurler syndrome but begins prenatally or at birth, with coarse facial features, marked gingival hypertrophy, congenital hip dislocation, joint contractures, hernias and severe growth failure.
Unlike the mucopolysaccharidoses, urinary glycosaminoglycan excretion is normal or only slightly raised, which helps separate the two groups.
Dysostosis multiplex, thoracic deformity, cardiac valve thickening and recurrent respiratory infection are usual, and psychomotor development is severely impaired.
The prognosis is poor, with death commonly occurring in early childhood from cardiorespiratory complications.
reference.pathophysiology: Newly synthesised soluble lysosomal hydrolases are normally tagged in the Golgi with mannose-6-phosphate, a marker recognised by receptors that divert the enzymes into the lysosomal pathway. The first and rate-limiting step in generating this tag is performed by the hexameric enzyme GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase, whose catalytic alpha and beta subunits are encoded by GNPTAB. In mucolipidosis II biallelic loss-of-function mutations abolish transferase activity, so the recognition marker cannot be added; the untagged hydrolases default to the constitutive secretory pathway and are released into the extracellular space and bloodstream. The lysosome is consequently starved of numerous hydrolases at once, and undegraded substrates accumulate as heterogeneous storage material within enlarged lysosomes throughout mesenchymal and other tissues. Because many enzymes are affected simultaneously, the disorder produces a widespread multisystem phenotype affecting bone, connective tissue, heart, airway and the developing nervous system, and the mislocalised enzymes can be measured at high levels in plasma, providing a diagnostic clue.
additionalDifferentials: Hurler syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis I) and other mucopolysaccharidoses
Infantile free sialic acid storage disease and other causes of neonatal dysostosis
additionalInvestigations: Plasma or serum lysosomal enzyme panel showing multiple hydrolases markedly elevated
Lysosomal enzyme assays in cultured skin fibroblasts showing reduced intracellular activity
Urinary glycosaminoglycan and oligosaccharide or sialyl-oligosaccharide screen
Echocardiography for valvular and myocardial involvement
Prenatal enzyme or molecular testing in at-risk pregnancies
redFlags: Congenital hip dislocation, joint contractures and coarse facial features present at birth
Failure to thrive accompanied by recurrent respiratory infection
Signs of cardiac valve disease or heart failure in infancy
Progressive respiratory compromise from thoracic and airway involvement
reference.prognosis: Mucolipidosis II is relentlessly progressive and life-limiting, with most affected children dying within the first years of life from cardiorespiratory failure; management is supportive.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the disorder as a mucopolysaccharidosis and being falsely reassured by normal urinary glycosaminoglycans.
Overlooking the diagnosis because it presents at birth, earlier than classic Hurler syndrome.
Failing to send both serum (elevated) and fibroblast (deficient) enzyme studies, which together are diagnostic.
Attributing the coarse features to congenital hypothyroidism alone.
Assuming that enzyme replacement or haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offers the benefit seen in some mucopolysaccharidoses, as evidence here is very limited.
